subject: Jacobian adjustment not caught by autodiff, how does Stan do it?

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Jacobian adjustment not caught by autodiff, how does Stan do it?
parts:
Dear all,

suppose an arbitrary model like in the manual as example of the jacobian adjustment:

data {
real<lower=0> y;
}
// ...
model {
log(y) ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

and later

target += - log(fabs(y));

How does Stan know this is part of a of adjustment, and do not add the 2nd derivative of log(y),
precisely I assumed that everything added to target is handled by Stans auto-derivation. Consequently
is d/dy - log(fabs(y)) is also added to the likelihood?

Andre

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Jacobian adjustment not caught by autodiff, how does Stan do it?
parts:
On Sunday, April 16, 2017 at 2:21:07 AM UTC-4, andre.p...@googlemail.com wrote:
data {
real<lower=0> y;
}
// ...
model {
log(y) ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

and later

target += - log(fabs(y));

How does Stan know this is part of a of adjustment, and do not add the 2nd derivative of log(y),

Stan knows that y is a constant array, so the derivatives are constants, so adding them to log posterior kernel would have no effect on the sampling, so Stan doesn't bother. You would be better off constructing log_y in the transformed data block and feeding log_y to the normal log-likelihood function.

messages.author: 3d7541308bd2e290
messages.subject: Re: Jacobian adjustment not caught by autodiff, how does Stan do it?
parts:
@BGoodrich

Since y is data here and isn't being sampled over, wouldn't it make sense to change this example?

In that model,

log(y) ~ normal(mu, sigma)


and

y ~ lognormal(y | mu, sigma)


*Are*, from a sampling perspective, equivalent. The log probabilities are a bit off, but whatever. I was looking at this transformed parameter stuff a couple days ago and that was bugging me.

I think it'd just make more sense to show a manually constrained sigma parameter. Here's a gist comparing the two lognormal examples: https://gist.github.com/bbbales2/2f68c4a9111284c0df8ad2f56505b495 . Here's a gist showing a manually constrained sigma variable: https://gist.github.com/bbbales2/34602cacc6cddeae68c68228670882f3 .

Also, and I don't know if this is what Andre was asking, but if this were a parameter and we wanted to enforce a lower bound constraint:

real<lower = 0.0> sigma;

Then if we wrote that in the model, Stan would already apply that transformation, and so manually adding an adjustment would be like a 2nd adjustment (dunno if that's what he's asking). In this case, the <lower=0.0> specification is in the data block so it's only used to verify the input data and there's no transform, but again, in this example it doesn't really matter :D.

As a side note, it might be worth referencing chapter 20 (especially section 20.3, Change of Variables) as well as 33.1 in this section. It's got a good discussion about the transformations where you need the Jacobian and the ones where you don't. (Also, @Andre, check out Section 20.3)

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Jacobian adjustment not caught by autodiff, how does Stan do it?
parts:
On Sunday, April 16, 2017 at 1:07:11 PM UTC-4, Ben B wrote:
@BGoodrich

Since y is data here and isn't being sampled over, wouldn't it make sense to change this example?

In that model,

log(y) ~ normal(mu, sigma)


and

y ~ lognormal(y | mu, sigma)


*Are*, from a sampling perspective, equivalent. The log probabilities are a bit off, but whatever. I was looking at this transformed parameter stuff a couple days ago and that was bugging me.
Using the lognormal function is less numerically stable than using the normal function on the logarithm of the outcome.

Also, and I don't know if this is what Andre was asking, but if this were a parameter and we wanted to enforce a lower bound constraint:

real<lower = 0.0> sigma;

Then if we wrote that in the model, Stan would already apply that transformation, and so manually adding an adjustment would be like a 2nd adjustment (dunno if that's what he's asking). In this case, the <lower=0.0> specification is in the data block so it's only used to verify the input data and there's no transform, but again, in this example it doesn't really matter :D.

For any constraints declared in the parameters block, Stan already does the Jacobian adjustment, in which case doing a second Jacobian adjustment would be wrong. For transformations in data or transformed data, no Jacobian adjustment is needed. If you use sampling statements, then Stan will warn you more than 100% of the time when a Jacobian adjustment is needed by the user. If you use target += statements, then Stan will not always warn you when a Jacobian adjustment is needed by the user.

Ben

Ben,

So the only way to get it wrong is, when y is a parameter, in for example in a latent approach.
As you say, in the case, where y is data it makes sense to use a data transformation. This
doesn't require the Jacobian adjustment, as it is a constant.

In the fist case, where y is parameter, however, do we have to correct the log-likelihood by
subtracting the derivative of the Jacobian transform of our parameter?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Jacobian adjustment not caught by autodiff, how does Stan do it?
parts:
For explicit Jacobian adjustments, it's the log of the absolute
value of the determinant of the Jacobian matrix.

You need the adjustment whenever you have a parameter theta
and you have a function f and want to define your distribution
on f(theta) and then pull it back so it does the right thing
on theta. Whereas if you have a variable theta and define the
density on theta, then f(theta) will be distributed correctly
without a Jacobian adjustment.

- Bob
